yt.description: The MOSFET in depth: N-channel enhancement MOSFET structure, threshold voltage VT, the square law ID = k(VGS - VT)^2, ohmic and saturation regions, enhancement vs depletion vs P-channel, voltage-divider biasing with every value calculated (ID 0.764 mA, VGS 3.24 V, VDS 6.04 V), transconductance and amplifier gain -8.4, and processor power stages.

scenes.title: THE MOSFET IN DEPTH
scenes.subtitle: Threshold, square law, regions and biasing
scenes.narration: Welcome back. Last time we compared MOSFETs with B J Ts. Today we go deep into the MOSFET itself: how its channel forms, the square law that governs its current, its two regions, the different types, and how to bias it as an amplifier, with every value calculated.

Our N channel enhancement MOSFET: P body, N plus source and drain, thin oxide, metal gate. Watch the gate voltage rise. Below two volts, the threshold, there's no channel, and no current. At two volts, a thin layer of electrons, called an inversion layer, forms under the gate. Above it, the channel deepens, and the current grows quickly.

Plot it: drain current against gate voltage. Zero below the threshold. Above it, the current follows a square law: I D equals k times V G S minus V T, squared. With k equal to zero point five milliamps per volt squared: at three volts, zero point five milliamps. At four volts, two milliamps. At six volts, eight milliamps.

The output curves. At low drain voltage, the MOSFET acts as a resistor whose value the gate controls: the ohmic region. That's where it's used as a switch. Once V D S exceeds V G S minus V T, the channel pinches off at the drain end, and the current levels off: the saturation region. There, it's a voltage controlled current source, perfect for amplifying.

There are four types. Our N channel enhancement MOSFET is normally off, and needs a positive gate voltage. A P channel enhancement MOSFET is its mirror: normally off, and needs a negative gate voltage. A depletion MOSFET is built with a channel already there, so it's normally on, and the gate voltage can increase or reduce the current. Enhancement N and P channel types are by far the most common, and together they make C M O S, as we'll see.

To use it as an amplifier, we bias it in saturation. A voltage divider, two megohms and one megohm, sets the gate at four volts. No gate current flows, so the divider isn't loaded at all, and we can use huge resistors. R S, one kilohm, in the source gives stability. R D, six point eight kilohms, in the drain. The result: zero point seven six milliamps, V G S three point two four volts, and V D S six point zero four volts.

Let's solve it. V G is twelve times one megohm over three megohms, four volts. V G S equals V G minus I D R S, four minus I D times one k. Put that into the square law: I D equals zero point five milliamps times two minus I D times one k, squared. The solution: I D is zero point seven six four milliamps. So V G S is four minus zero point seven six four, three point two four volts. V D S equals twelve minus zero point seven six four times seven point eight k, six point zero four volts. Check saturation: V D S, six, is bigger than V G S minus V T, one point two four. Yes. The transconductance g m is two k times V G S minus V T, one point two four milliamps per volt. Gain: minus g m R D, minus eight point four.

The buck converters that feed your laptop's processor are built from MOSFETs. They switch tens of amps, hundreds of thousands of times a second, with only milliohms of resistance when on. And the processor itself is built from billions of tiny MOSFETs. The MOSFET is the most manufactured device in human history.

Three common mistakes. One: using the square law in the ohmic region. It only applies in saturation, when V D S is at least V G S minus V T. Always check. Two: forgetting that the gate current is zero. With MOSFETs, the divider voltage is exact, no loading. Three: expecting MOSFET amplifiers to match B J T gain. Their transconductance is lower at the same current, so a single stage gives less gain.

scenes.title: NEXT: MOSFET NUMERICALS
scenes.narration: Quick recap. A MOSFET's channel forms above the threshold voltage. In saturation, I D equals k times V G S minus V T squared. Bias it with a divider, which the gate doesn't load, and a source resistor. The gain is minus g m R D, with g m equal to two k times V G S minus V T. Next, MOSFET numericals, solved step by step. See you there.

short_scenes.narration: How does a MOSFET turn on? Raise the gate voltage. Above two volts, the threshold, electrons gather under the gate and form a channel. No channel, no current. Channel, current.
And the current follows a square law: k times V G S minus V T, squared. Three volts, half a milliamp. Four volts, two milliamps. Six volts, eight.
Below pinch off, it's a resistor, used as a switch. Above, it's a current source, used as an amplifier. That's the MOSFET. Full lesson on the channel.
